summary: Defines the protocol for the L4S network service. It uses an Explicit Congestion Notification scheme at the IP layer that is similar to classic ECN but gives much more frequent signals, matched to scalable congestion control. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers can put a small mark on packets saying getting crowded. L4S uses lots of tiny marks, so senders adjust gently and quickly.

questions: what is the l4s ecn codepoint
how does l4s ecn differ from classic ecn
what is a scalable congestion control
subtitle: Using the ECT(1) codepoint in the IP header to flag traffic that wants frequent congestion marks and very low queuing delay.

tldr.problem: Classic congestion control makes queues swing and does not scale well to high speeds, so applications that need both high throughput and low delay suffer, and network queues cannot tell Scalable traffic from Classic traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A sender sets the ECT(1) codepoint in the IP ECN field to say it uses a Scalable congestion control. Network nodes classify ECT(1) and CE packets into a separate low-latency treatment and mark them with CE immediately and frequently, while senders respond in small, smoothed steps.
tldr.outcome: The experiment aims at sub-millisecond average queuing delay without losing link utilization. It is Experimental, and its open questions are collected in the RFC.

facts.label: Reported queuing delay
facts.value: Sub-millisecond average, about 1 to 2 ms at the 99th percentile

today: RFC 9331 is an Experimental RFC from January 2023 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is one part of the L4S work alongside the architecture in RFC 9330 and the queue design in RFC 9332.

sections.title: The Latency and Scaling Problem
sections.content:
This Experimental specification defines the protocol for a network service called Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable throughput (L4S). It uses an Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) scheme at the IP layer with the same codepoint transitions as Classic ECN in RFC 3168. That RFC requires a mark to be equivalent to a drop. L4S differs in two ways: the network marks more immediately and more frequently than it would drop, and the transport reduces its response to each mark. The two changes counterbalance, so an L4S flow gets roughly the same throughput as a comparable non-L4S flow.

The RFC argues that Classic congestion controls sawtooth, and the additional queuing delay at the tips is of the same order as the base round-trip time, even with a well-tuned AQM. Classic controls such as Reno and CUBIC also approach their scaling limits. Scalable congestion controls use much smaller sawtooth variations, and the average time between congestion signals stays the same as flow rate grows. DCTCP is an example, but it is applicable solely to controlled environments such as data centres.
sections.plainLanguage: Big swings in speed make queues long. Many tiny adjustments keep the line short, even when traffic grows.

sections.title: The L4S Identifier
sections.content:
The identifier is the ECT(1) codepoint of the 2-bit IP ECN field (binary 01), together with CE. The four codepoints keep the names from RFC 3168: Not-ECT, ECT(0), ECT(1) and CE. After assessing alternatives, the RFC chose this as the best compromise against a list of SHOULD-level requirements: it should survive end to end, be visible at the IP layer, work for IPv4 and IPv6 and any transport, be incrementally deployable and use minimal extra codepoints.

The identifier applies to IPv4 and IPv6, and to unicast, multicast and anycast forwarding. It is orthogonal to the Differentiated Services Code Point. Because the document is Experimental, it relies on RFC 8311, which lets Experimental RFCs relax the rule that an ECN mark must be equivalent to a drop. The overall architecture is in RFC 9330, and the queue design in RFC 9332.
sections.plainLanguage: The special tap uses one particular secret handshake in the packet's header, so routers can spot who wants the gentle treatment.

sections.title: What Senders Must Do
sections.content:
A sender that wants L4S treatment MUST set ECT(1). It needs transport feedback that reports the extent of CE marking, not just one mark per round trip. The RFC gives the position for TCP (accurate ECN feedback, such as AccECN), SCTP, RTP over UDP, QUIC and DCCP.

Before sending ECT(1), a host SHOULD use a Scalable congestion control: the average time between induced marks must not grow as flow rate scales. For DCTCP, TCP Prague and the L4S variant of SCReAM the average recovery time is half a round trip, equivalent to 2 marks per round trip. Further numbered requirements say the control MUST be replaceable by a Classic one, MUST react to packet loss in a way that coexists safely with Reno, and MUST be monitored in uncontrolled environments to detect a Classic ECN AQM in a shared queue. If problems are detected and not resolved, the sender MUST revert to a Classic congestion control.

The RFC notes that in the worst case tested, throughput could favour an L4S flow over a Classic one by 25:1 in a shared Classic ECN queue, which is why detection and fallback matter.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want the fast lane, you must promise to slow down in small steps, and to switch to normal rules if the road turns out to be an ordinary one.

sections.title: What Network Nodes Must Do
sections.content:
A node that implements L4S MUST classify arriving ECT(1) packets, and by default CE packets, for L4S treatment. It MUST NOT change ECT(1) to any codepoint other than CE, and MUST NOT change CE to anything else. Under persistent overload it MUST drop L4S traffic with the same drop probability as Classic traffic. For backward compatibility it MUST also provide a Classic AQM, classifying ECT(0) and Not-ECT packets there, and it MUST be possible to disable L4S treatment, in which case ECT(1) is treated as Not-ECT.

L4S marking is not smoothed, so the node signals congestion as soon as possible. Where queues are not scheduled per flow, the likelihood of dropping a Classic packet (p_C) MUST be roughly proportional to the square of the L4S marking likelihood (p_L), written p_C ~= (p_L / k)^2, with k = 2 RECOMMENDED. That squaring balances Reno's square-root response so both kinds of flow converge to roughly equal congestion windows.

Operators may add other identifiers, such as address ranges or Diffserv codepoints, to put safe low-rate traffic like DNS or voice in the low-latency queue, or to exclude traffic from L4S treatment. A node MUST NOT swap Not-ECT or ECT(0) into an L4S identifier, nor change L4S to Classic.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers give the special tap to anyone with the right sign, never fake the sign, and still keep a normal lane for everyone else.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
IANA has updated the 01 entry of the ECN Field (Bits 6-7) registry to ECT(1) (ECN-Capable Transport(1)), referencing RFC 8311 and RFC 9331. The assignment of the codepoint's semantics is allowed by RFC 8311.

The RFC points out that defining ECT(1) as the L4S identifier makes ECT(0) and ECT(1) differ in effect, though RFC 3168 treated them as equivalent. Nodes are still required not to swap one for the other. A malicious node that did so could make a flow yield excessively or be marked by a Classic AQM.

A second concern is VPNs. If the anti-replay window of a VPN egress is too small, it may mistake delay differences between L4S and Classic packets for replay and discard packets. An attacker could exploit this against a user who has set up a VPN carelessly, and the RFC recommends a sufficiently large anti-replay window. Detecting loss in time units prevents ACK-splitting attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody may secretly change the signs on packets, and secret tunnels must be wide enough that delayed packets are not thrown away by mistake.
